desc:
The rotations of a string s are the strings obtained by moving some number of leading characters (0 up to n - 1) to the back. Different shifts can give the same rotation (for "abab" there are only two distinct rotations).

Return how many distinct rotations of s are lexicographically smaller than s itself.

s = "bab"      rotations: bab, abb, bba      result = 1
s = "baba"     distinct: baba, abab          result = 1
s = "abab"                                   result = 0
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Building all rotations and sorting them is too slow for long strings: there are n rotations of length n each.

Rotation i is (s+s)[i : i+n]. To compare it with s you only need the length of their longest common prefix, then one character comparison. The Z-function of s + '#' + s + s gives all those prefix lengths at once.
Rotations repeat with period p, the smallest i ≥ 1 for which rotation i equals s (or n if there is none). Count the rotations i in 1..p-1 that are smaller than s; each of those is a different string.
editorial: Let d = s + s. Rotation i is d[i : i+n]. Compute the Z-function of s + '#' + d: the value at the position of d[i] is the length of the longest common prefix l of rotation i and s (the separator stops matches at n). If l = n the rotation equals s; otherwise rotation i is smaller than s exactly when d[i + l] < s[l].

The sequence of rotations repeats every p steps, where p is the first i ≥ 1 with rotation i equal to s (and p = n when the string is not periodic). So the distinct rotations are exactly rotations 0..p-1; rotation 0 is s itself, and the answer is the number of i in 1..p-1 whose rotation is smaller. Time O(n), space O(n).
